questions.question: You insert 2, then 3, then 4 into a stack, and the same three values in the same order into a queue. Then you remove all elements from each. In what order do they come out?
options: Stack: 2, 3, 4 — Queue: 4, 3, 2
Stack: 4, 3, 2 — Queue: 2, 3, 4
Stack: 4, 3, 2 — Queue: 4, 3, 2
Stack: 2, 3, 4 — Queue: 2, 3, 4
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out): insertion and removal happen at the top, so 4 leaves first. A queue is FIFO (first in, first out): elements enter at the back and leave from the front, like people in a line, so 2 leaves first. The first option simply swaps the two behaviours.

questions.question: You need to store each student's roll number against their name (Aditya → 101, Rohit → 102) and fetch a roll number by name in constant time on average. Names are unique. Which kind of structure from the lecture fits?
options: A Set, because it rejects duplicate names
A Queue, because students are registered in order
A List, because it stores elements by index
A Map such as HashMap, because it stores key → value pairs looked up by key
questions.explanation: A Map associates a unique key with a value and, when hash-based, finds the value by hashing the key into a bucket in O(1) on average. A Set does reject duplicates, but it stores single elements, not name → roll-number pairs. A List would need a linear O(N) search by name.

questions.question: Why does the lecture build a `DynamicArray` (the idea behind `ArrayList`) instead of just using `int[] arr = new int[10];`?
options: A plain array has a fixed size (writing `arr[10]` fails), while a dynamic array creates a bigger array and copies the elements when it fills up
A plain array cannot store primitive values like `int`, while a dynamic array can
A plain array has no index-based access, while a dynamic array provides `get(int index)`
A plain array is stored on the stack, while a dynamic array is the only way to store data on the heap
questions.explanation: An array's length is fixed at creation, so with length 10 the valid indexes are 0–9 and `arr[10]` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. A dynamic array hides this: when it is full, it allocates a larger array and copies existing elements, so `add()` keeps working. Plain arrays do store primitives and do offer O(1) index access, so those options are false.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Initially 4 → 5. `n3.ref = n1.ref` makes 8 point to 5, then `n1.ref = n3` makes 4 point to 8, giving 4 → 8 → 5 → null. This is the lecture's insertion-in-the-middle idea: no elements are shifted, only references change. If the two lines were swapped, n3 would end up pointing to itself and the loop would never end.

questions.question: This is the lecture's simple hash-based set (no chaining yet). What does it print?
options: true true true
false true true
true false true
An ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown for 100
questions.explanation: `el % arr.length` always yields an index 0–9, so 100 does not go out of bounds: it maps to index 0, the same bucket as 10, and overwrites it. Hence `contains(10)` is false, `contains(100)` true and `contains(12)` (index 2) true. This collision is exactly why real HashSet/HashMap keep a chain of nodes per bucket instead of a single slot.

questions.question: A teammate wrote `ArrayList<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>();` and passes `l` to many methods typed `ArrayList<Integer>`. Later you want to try `LinkedList` instead. Which design, shown in the lecture, makes that switch a one-line change?
options: Declare the variable and parameters as the interface type `List<Integer>`, so only `new ArrayList<>()` needs to change to `new LinkedList<>()`
Make `LinkedList` extend `ArrayList` so it can be passed wherever an `ArrayList` is expected
Declare everything as `Object` and cast to the right class wherever `add()` is called
Copy the elements into a new array each time a method needs a different list type
questions.explanation: `ArrayList` and `LinkedList` both implement the `List` interface, so coding against `List<Integer>` lets polymorphism pick the right `add()`/`remove()` at runtime. Only the object creation changes. You cannot change JDK class hierarchies, and declaring everything as `Object` throws away type safety and forces casts.

questions.question: In the hierarchy drawn in the lecture, `Collection` is the root interface. Which of these is NOT a sub-interface of `Collection`?
options: `List`
`Set`
`Queue`
`Map`
questions.explanation: `List`, `Set` and `Queue` all extend `Collection`, which models a group of single elements. `Map` stores key → value pairs, so its operations (put by key, get by key) don't fit Collection's `add(element)` contract and it is a separate hierarchy. `Set` is a common wrong pick because a Map's keys behave like a set, but `Set` itself does extend `Collection`.

questions.question: A leaderboard loads 1 million scores once, then the app reads scores by position (`get(i)` with random `i`) millions of times; insertions in the middle are rare. Based on how a dynamic array and a linked list store data, which is the better choice and why?
options: A linked list, because each node knows its neighbour, so jumping to position i is O(1)
A linked list, because it never has to resize, which makes every read faster
A dynamic array (ArrayList), because elements sit in contiguous indexes so `get(i)` is O(1), while a linked list must walk node by node
Either one, because both are Lists and therefore have identical performance for every operation
questions.explanation: A dynamic array stores elements in an underlying array, so reading index i is a direct O(1) access. A linked list only knows the head and each node's `next`, so reaching position i costs O(i). Linked lists shine when you insert by relinking references without shifting, which this workload rarely needs; sharing the `List` interface does not make their performance identical.

questions.question: In the lecture's hash-based set, both 10 and 100 land in bucket 0 (`el % 10`). How does chaining resolve this, and what does it mean for lookup cost?
options: The second value is moved to the next empty index, so lookup is always exactly O(1)
Each bucket holds a linked chain of nodes; `contains` hashes to the bucket then walks that chain, so lookup is O(1) on average but degrades if many values share one bucket
The array is resized whenever any two values collide, so no bucket ever holds more than one value
The colliding value is rejected as a duplicate, because two values with the same bucket are considered equal
questions.explanation: With chaining, a bucket stores a small linked list (10 → 100); lookup computes the bucket from the hash and then compares only the few nodes in that chain. With a good hash spread the chains stay short, giving average O(1), but if many values collide into one bucket the walk becomes long. Treating colliding values as duplicates would be wrong — 10 and 100 are different values that merely share a bucket.

questions.question: This mini dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. What does it print?
questions.explanation: Capacity starts at 2: adding 4 and 10 fills it; adding 13 doubles it to 4; 15 fits; adding 17 finds size 4 == length 4 and doubles to 8. So capacity is 8, size is 5, and `arr[4]` is 17. The tempting "5 5 17" confuses capacity (`arr.length`) with the number of stored elements (`size`).
